Two Kinds of Many-to-Many →

Two Relations, One Table

A ticket's customer and its assigned agent are both a User — Prisma needs a name to tell the two relations apart.

A ticket also has an assigned agent — nullable, since a ticket can sit unassigned — and an agent is a User too, exactly like the customer. That's two separate 1:M relationships from Ticket landing on the same User table, which is where the previous slide's plain @relation stops being enough: given two of them, Prisma has no way to tell which User field pairs with which. Figure 2.7 shows how the real schema resolves it.

// Figure 2.7: two named relations on one table (prisma/schema.prisma, excerpt)
model Ticket {
  customerId      Int
  assignedAgentId Int?

  customer      User  @relation("CustomerTickets", fields: [customerId], references: [id])
  assignedAgent User? @relation("AssignedTickets", fields: [assignedAgentId], references: [id])
}

model User {
  ticketsAsCustomer Ticket[] @relation("CustomerTickets")
  ticketsAsAgent    Ticket[] @relation("AssignedTickets")
}

The string — "CustomerTickets", "AssignedTickets" — is a relation name, existing purely to pair up the two ends of each relation explicitly; it's never stored anywhere or seen again outside the schema file. Every @relation needs one the moment there's more than one path between the same two models — here, Ticket.customer pairs with User.ticketsAsCustomer, and Ticket.assignedAgent pairs with User.ticketsAsAgent, each by matching name. assignedAgentId Int? and assignedAgent User? — the trailing ? — mark both as nullable, Prisma's way of saying "this relation might not exist for a given row," which lines up with a ticket genuinely having no agent yet.
